WASHINGTON (CNN) -- As tensions over Iran's disputed presidential election continue to escalate, President Obama should reach out to opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi, a former Bush administration official told CNN on Sunday.

Paul Wolfowitz, who served as deputy defense secretary under President Bush, addressed the matter in an interview with CNN's Wolf Blitzer. "I would certainly find out if he [Moussavi] wants a conversation," Wolfowitz said. "If he doesn't, I certainly wouldn't push it. But I would make it clear that the phone is an open line."

On Saturday, Obama issued a written statement addressing the bloodshed unfolding in the streets of Tehran, where demonstrators have taken to protesting the election results. "The Iranian government must understand that the world is watching," he said. "We mourn each and every innocent life that is lost. We call on the Iranian government to stop all violent and unjust actions against its own people. The universal rights to assembly and free speech must be respected, and the United States stands with all who seek to exercise those rights."

Nevertheless, Obama has drawn criticism from some lawmakers and analysts who contend he should adopt a firmer public stance on the unrest.

Watch the latest videos emerging from Iran »

"I understand the concern about meddling in a way that seems to label the opposition as American tools, but the opposition has made it very clear that they want support from the world," said Wolfowitz, a staunch advocate of the U.S.-led war in Iraq and currently a scholar at the American Enterprise Institute.

CNN Senior Political Analyst David Gergen echoed this sentiment, noting, "It would be useful for the president to show more forceful leadership internationally on this issue." Pointing to the graphic images emerging from Iran—including footage of the fatal shooting of a young female protester identified as Neda—Gergen argued that such violence demands "some kind of humanity from the West."

Both Gergen and Wolfowitz suggested that the United States should join forces with other Western nations, and even with countries in the region such as Afghanistan and Turkey—both of which have recognized incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the victor of the June 12 election—to stand in solidarity with the Iranian people.

Ahmadinejad's declared victory, certified by Iran's Guardian Council, ignited massive protests last week, with many demonstrators voicing their support for Moussavi. Both Moussavi and fellow candidate Mehdi Karrubi have denounced the election as fraudulent and called for a new vote.

Wolfowitz praised Moussavi as "a very brave man," adding, "He is resisting. He is putting his life at risk."

"I would definitely check whether he wants to talk," Wolfowitz explained regarding Moussavi. "If he declines, I wouldn't press the matter. But I'd make sure he knows the line of communication remains open."

"I understand the concern about meddling in a way that seems to label the opposition as American tools, but the opposition made it very clear they want support from the world," he said.

David Gergen, CNN's senior political analyst, echoed similar sentiments, suggesting that "it would be useful for the president to show more forceful leadership internationally on this issue." Referring to disturbing footage coming out of Iran—including the death of a young female demonstrator named Neda who was shot—Gergen argued the bloodshed demands "some kind of humanity from the West."

Both Gergen and Wolfowitz urged the United States to join forces with other Western allies, as well as regional nations like Afghanistan and Turkey—both of which have already acknowledged Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the election's victor—in showing solidarity with the Iranian population.

Iran's Guardian Council, the country's electoral authority, certified Ahmadinejad's win, triggering widespread demonstrations the previous week, with countless protesters voicing their backing for Moussavi. Both Moussavi and fellow candidate Mehdi Karrubi have dismissed the election results as illegitimate, calling for the vote to be redone.

Wolfowitz praised Moussavi as "a very brave man," adding, "He is resisting. He is putting his life at risk."

# U.S. Response to Iranian Election Unrest: Calls for Stronger Engagement

As post-election tensions escalated dramatically in Iran, former Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz called on President Obama to take a more proactive diplomatic approach by reaching out directly to Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi. Wolfowitz argued that establishing this line of communication was a critical step the administration should consider, given the gravity of the unfolding crisis and the opposition movement's growing significance on the world stage.

In articulating his position, Wolfowitz was careful to balance the need for U.S. engagement with sensitivity to the political realities on the ground in Iran. He suggested that Obama should simply make clear to Moussavi that an open channel of communication was available, without imposing any expectation of immediate contact. This approach, Wolfowitz noted, would respect Moussavi's own judgment about whether and when engaging with the United States would serve the opposition movement's interests, avoiding the risk of the U.S. involvement becoming a liability that the Iranian government could exploit for propaganda purposes.

For his part, President Obama did respond to the escalating violence in Tehran through an official statement, in which he condemned the crackdown and called on the Iranian government to respect the fundamental rights of its citizens to peaceful assembly and free speech. Obama urged Iranian authorities to cease violent actions against protesters, framing the unrest as a matter of basic human rights rather than solely a political dispute over the election's legitimacy.

Despite this statement, Obama's response drew criticism from some lawmakers and political analysts who felt the administration's public posture remained too measured given the severity of the crackdown. CNN's David Gergen was among those voicing concern, arguing that the situation demanded more forceful and visible international leadership from the United States. Gergen suggested that a stronger, more assertive stance was necessary to signal solidarity with the Iranian people and to hold the government accountable for its actions.

Both Wolfowitz and Gergen converged on a broader point: that the United States needed to work in concert with Western allies and other nations to mount a unified international response to the crisis. This call for collective action gained additional urgency following the release of graphic footage documenting the violence, most notably the death of Neda Agha-Soltan, a young woman whose killing during a protest became a galvanizing symbol of the government's brutal response to dissent. Her death, captured on video and widely circulated, intensified international scrutiny and added pressure on world leaders to move beyond statements of concern toward more coordinated diplomatic action.

# Wolfowitz Urges Obama to Open Direct Line to Iranian Opposition Leader

As post-election violence continued to intensify across Iran, former Bush administration official Paul Wolfowitz called on President Obama to establish a direct communication channel with opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi, arguing that a carefully calibrated approach could demonstrate American solidarity with Iranian protesters without giving the ruling regime ammunition to portray the unrest as a foreign-orchestrated conspiracy.

Speaking on the escalating crisis, Wolfowitz suggested that reaching out to Moussavi—even through informal or back-channel means—would send an unmistakable signal of support to those risking their lives in the streets of Tehran, while still allowing the administration to maintain that it was not meddling in Iran's internal affairs. "There are ways to show whose side we're on without becoming the story ourselves," Wolfowitz said, emphasizing that silence or excessive caution could be interpreted as indifference to the protesters' plight.

The push for a bolder American response came in the wake of President Obama's written statement, which condemned the violence unfolding in Iran following the disputed election but stopped short of explicitly endorsing Moussavi or directly challenging the legitimacy of the vote. The president's carefully worded remarks reflected the administration's delicate balancing act: expressing concern for human rights and the safety of demonstrators while avoiding language that could be exploited by Iranian authorities to frame the unrest as an American-backed effort to destabilize the government.

That measured approach drew criticism from multiple corners, including from Wolfowitz and CNN senior political analyst David Gergen, both of whom argued that the moment called for more forceful and visible American leadership. Gergen contended that the United States, as a global champion of democratic values, had a responsibility to speak out unequivocally in defense of the Iranian people's fundamental rights to free speech and peaceful assembly, rights that were being violently suppressed as security forces cracked down on demonstrators.

Critics of the administration's cautious posture argued that history would judge the moment harshly if Washington failed to stand more visibly with those demanding accountability and transparency in their government. They pointed to the scale of the protests—among the largest Iran had seen in decades—as evidence that the world was witnessing a pivotal moment in the country's political trajectory, one that demanded clear moral clarity from American leadership rather than diplomatic hedging.

Supporters of Obama's approach, however, defended the administration's restraint, warning that overt American involvement could backfire, potentially undermining the very movement it sought to support by allowing the Iranian government to cast the protests as externally manipulated rather than an authentic expression of domestic discontent. This tension between the desire to support democratic aspirations and the risk of counterproductive intervention would continue to shape the administration's messaging as the situation in Iran unfolded in the days that followed.

# Wolfowitz Urges Obama to Publicly Back Iranian Opposition Leader Mousavi

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Former Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz called on President Obama Tuesday to more forcefully support Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Mousavi, arguing that the administration's cautious response to the disputed election and subsequent crackdown risks putting the United States "on the wrong side of history."

Wolfowitz, an architect of the Bush administration's foreign policy who now serves as a scholar at the American Enterprise Institute, said in an interview that Obama should use his platform to explicitly validate the protesters' claims of election fraud and voice support for Mousavi as the legitimate representative of Iranian voters' will.

"This is a moment when the United States needs to stand clearly with the Iranian people, not with a regime that appears to be stealing an election in broad daylight," Wolfowitz said. "Reaching out to Mousavi, even symbolically, would send an unmistakable signal about where America stands."

The comments come as hundreds of thousands of Iranians have taken to the streets of Tehran and other cities to protest the official results of the June 12 election, which handed a decisive victory to incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad over Mousavi. International observers and opposition supporters have alleged widespread irregularities, and the demonstrations have grown into the largest challenge to the Islamic Republic's leadership since the 1979 revolution.

Obama has walked a careful line in his public statements, expressing concern over the violence used against protesters while stopping short of directly endorsing Mousavi or declaring the election fraudulent. The administration has said it does not want to be seen as meddling in Iran's internal affairs, wary that overt American support for the opposition could be used by the Iranian government to discredit the protest movement as a foreign-backed plot.

"I understand the argument that too much American involvement could backfire," Wolfowitz said. "But there's a difference between meddling and moral clarity. The Iranian people are the ones showing extraordinary courage here — they don't need us to run their revolution, but they do need to know America isn't indifferent to whether their votes were counted."

Wolfowitz's remarks reflect a broader debate playing out among foreign policy commentators and lawmakers in Washington. Republican critics, including Senator John McCain, have accused Obama of being too muted in his response, while some Democrats and Iran analysts have warned that aggressive rhetoric from Washington could play into the hands of hardliners in Tehran looking to paint the unrest as externally orchestrated.

White House officials have pushed back on the criticism, noting that Obama has repeatedly said he is "deeply troubled" by the images of violence coming out of Iran, including the death of a young woman, Neda Agha-Soltan, whose killing was captured on video and quickly spread worldwide, becoming a symbol of the crackdown.

"The president has been clear that the world is watching, and that the Iranian government will be held accountable for its actions," White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs said Monday. "But this is fundamentally a struggle for the Iranian people to wage themselves."

Wolfowitz, who was a leading proponent of the Iraq War and has long argued for a more assertive American role in promoting democracy in the Middle East, dismissed concerns that a statement of support for Mousavi would play into the regime's hands.

"The Iranian government is already calling this a foreign conspiracy, no matter what we do or don't say," he said. "So the question isn't whether they'll blame us — they will regardless. The question is whether we stand up clearly for the principle that people have a right to have their votes counted."

He added that Obama's own history — including his Cairo speech earlier this month calling for a new relationship with the Muslim world — gave him unique credibility to speak out.

"He has enormous moral authority right now," Wolfowitz said. "This is the moment to use it."

The White House has given no indication it plans to shift its approach, with officials emphasizing that the administration remains focused on preserving the possibility of future diplomatic engagement with Tehran over its nuclear program, a priority that could be complicated by a more openly confrontational stance toward the government during the unrest.

As the protests continue and the Iranian government intensifies its crackdown on demonstrators, journalists and social media, the pressure on Obama to clarify his position is likely to persist — from Wolfowitz and other voices across the political spectrum.

# Reactions to Obama's Response to Iran's 2009 Post-Election Violence

In June 2009, following Iran's disputed presidential election and the subsequent crackdown on protesters, President Obama faced criticism from various quarters for his cautious, measured response. Here's a summary of the reactions:

## Criticism from Former Bush Officials

Former Bush administration officials and Republican voices generally argued that Obama was:
- **Too timid/passive** in condemning the Iranian government's violent crackdown on protesters
- **Failing to clearly side with the demonstrators** seeking democratic reforms
- **Prioritizing potential nuclear negotiations** with Tehran over supporting a democratic uprising
- Missing an opportunity to align with what many saw as a historic pro-democracy movement, similar to how Reagan was credited with supporting dissidents in the Soviet bloc

Critics like former UN Ambassador John Bolton and other Bush-era foreign policy figures argued that Obama's restraint signaled weakness and a reluctance to challenge authoritarian regimes.

## CNN Analyst Perspectives

CNN analysts and commentators were more mixed, generally falling into two camps:
- **Some agreed with the criticism**, suggesting Obama's cautious approach missed a moral moment
- **Others defended Obama's strategy**, arguing that:
  - Overt US involvement or strong statements could backfire, allowing the Iranian regime to portray protesters as American puppets
  - This would give Tehran justification to crack down harder while discrediting the opposition movement
  - A measured approach was more pragmatic given the complicated history of US-Iran relations (including the 1953 coup)

## Obama's Response and Evolution

Obama initially struck a cautious tone, expressing concern but avoiding direct interference rhetoric. As the violence escalated (including the killing of Neda Agha-Soltan, which became a symbol of the protests), Obama's language grew somewhat stronger, condemning the violence more explicitly while still avoiding language that suggested the U.S. was directing or orchestrating the opposition.

---

Critics from across the political spectrum suggested the administration's measured tone—aimed at avoiding the appearance of American interference—may have undercut the moral clarity many expected from Washington during a pivotal moment for the Iranian opposition movement.

"This is a moment to speak clearly about what is at stake for the Iranian people," Wolfowitz said, contending that the administration's careful diplomatic language risked signaling indifference at a critical juncture when protesters were putting themselves at risk.

Gergen's comments captured a tension running through much of the criticism: acknowledging the legitimate diplomatic complexities Obama faced while still pressing for a more assertive posture.

The White House defended its approach, with officials noting that any perception of U.S. involvement could be used by Iranian authorities to discredit the protest movement as foreign-instigated, potentially providing cover for a harsher crackdown.

# Calls Mount for U.S. to Back Iranian Protesters Amid Disputed Election Fallout

In the wake of Iran's contested June 2009 presidential election, which saw incumbent Mahmoud Ahmadinejad declared the winner over reformist challenger Mir-Hossein Mousavi amid widespread allegations of fraud, a fierce debate has emerged in Washington over how forcefully the United States should support the demonstrators who have taken to the streets of Tehran and other Iranian cities.

## A Cautious White House Response

President Obama's initial reaction to the unrest was notably measured. Speaking in the days following the election, Obama stated that "the difference between Ahmadinejad and Mousavi in terms of their actual policies may not be as great as has been advertised," while emphasizing that "it's not productive, given the history of U.S.-Iranian relations, to be seen as meddling."

As protests intensified and reports of violent crackdowns emerged, Obama's tone shifted somewhat. He condemned the "violence perpetrated against them" and declared himself "appalled and outraged" by the treatment of demonstrators, while still maintaining that the U.S. should avoid being cast as instigating the unrest—a narrative Iranian officials were already pushing to delegitimize the protest movement.

## Critics Push for Stronger Statements

The administration's careful posture drew sharp criticism from multiple directions.

Conservative commentators and some foreign policy hawks argued that Obama's restraint amounted to moral abdication. Senator John McCain, among others, urged the president to speak with greater clarity in solidarity with protesters, suggesting that muted rhetoric from Washington could be read by the Iranian regime—and by the demonstrators themselves—as indifference to their cause.

Editorial pages and foreign policy analysts pressed the case that the U.S. had a moral obligation to vocally support a democratic movement, regardless of diplomatic complications. Some argued that historical memory mattered here: the U.S. role in the 1953 coup that toppled Iran's democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh gave Washington additional reason to tread carefully, but others countered that this history shouldn't paralyze the U.S. from clearly backing democratic aspirations decades later.

## The Meddling Dilemma

Supporters of Obama's approach countered that any overt U.S. backing could backfire spectacularly, handing the Iranian government a propaganda tool to paint the protests as a foreign-orchestrated plot rather than an organic expression of domestic discontent. Iranian state media had already begun floating claims of Western interference, and administration officials worried that heightened American rhetoric would only reinforce these narratives, potentially undermining the very movement the U.S. sought to help.

This tension—between the impulse to voice solidarity with a democratic uprising and the fear of tainting that uprising through association with a distrusted external power—came to define the debate. Officials at the State Department reportedly grappled with striking language that expressed concern for the demonstrators without providing Tehran ammunition to reframe the story as one of American meddling rather than Iranian self-determination.

## An Unresolved Tension

As the situation on the ground continued to evolve, with reports of casualties among protesters and communications crackdowns making information difficult to verify, the debate in Washington remained unsettled. The administration continued to calibrate its statements carefully, walking the line between expressing support for what it called "universal values" of free expression and assembly, and avoiding language that could be construed as directing or orchestrating the opposition movement.

Whether this approach would prove prescient or overly cautious remained, for observers across the political spectrum, an open question—one intertwined with deeper uncertainties about the trajectory of the protests themselves and their ultimate impact on Iran's political future.

---

*This piece reflects the developing and contested narrative around U.S. policy responses in the immediate aftermath of Iran's 2009 election crisis.*

**Iran's Election Crisis: Washington Treads Carefully as Unrest Grows**

*CNN*

Washington is walking a diplomatic tightrope as it responds to the escalating post-election turmoil in Iran, with officials debating how vocal the United States should be in supporting protesters while avoiding accusations of foreign interference that could undermine the opposition movement itself.

The soul-searching in Washington comes as disturbing images and video continue to emerge from Tehran, including footage of a young woman named Neda Agha-Soltan, who was fatally shot during protests and has since become a haunting symbol of the crackdown on dissent. Her death, captured on cellphone video and circulated widely online, has galvanized international sympathy for the demonstrators and intensified scrutiny of the Iranian government's response to unrest following the disputed re-election of President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.

Opposition candidate Mir Hossein Moussavi, who has rejected the official election results as fraudulent, has continued to defy government pressure, urging his supporters to keep demonstrating despite warnings from authorities. His refusal to back down has emboldened protesters even as the Iranian government has moved to restrict foreign media access and crack down on communications, including social media platforms that have become crucial tools for organizing and sharing information with the outside world.

President Obama has faced criticism from some quarters for what critics call a measured, cautious response to the unfolding crisis. The administration has expressed concern over the violence and voiced support for the universal rights of free expression and assembly, but has stopped short of explicitly siding with the opposition or calling for a new election.

Administration officials argue that a more forceful U.S. stance could backfire, potentially allowing the Iranian government to paint the protests as a Western-orchestrated plot rather than a genuine domestic uprising. Iran's leadership has a long history of accusing the United States of meddling in its internal affairs, and officials worry that aggressive rhetoric from Washington could hand the regime a convenient narrative to discredit the demonstrators.

"There's a fine line between expressing support for basic human rights and appearing to orchestrate or encourage regime change from the outside," said one State Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity. "We have to be mindful of the history here."

Still, some lawmakers on Capitol Hill, from both parties, have pushed for a stronger condemnation of the Iranian government's tactics, arguing that the U.S. has a moral obligation to speak out clearly against the violence, particularly in light of images like Neda's death that have shocked global audiences.

The debate underscores the delicate balancing act facing the Obama administration: voicing solidarity with Iranians demanding accountability and transparency while avoiding actions that could be construed as interference in what remains, fundamentally, an internal political struggle.

As the situation on the ground remains fluid and access to independent reporting inside Iran remains severely limited, the world continues to watch closely — with Neda's death and Moussavi's defiant stand serving as powerful symbols of a movement that shows no signs of retreating.

*CNN will continue to follow developments as this story unfolds.*
